deep.reconstruction: There is no mathematics on this page. It is a fair-copy page of lecture or study notes on ancient Persian history, continuing the narrative of the previous page (Artaxerxes I, Xerxes II, Sogdianus, Darius II). The page covers the following points. Artaxerxes II Mnemon is described as a good-natured man whom his many wives (or advisers) made a good man 'but not a prince'. His brother Cyrus the Younger is said to be only 15 but among the most ambitious princes; as a boy he had received rule over Asia Minor (Vorderasien) and now sought the throne. After Darius II's death Cyrus plotted against his brother and would have paid with his life had their mother (Parysatis) not interceded. Back in his satrapy he resumed his plan, raised an army of 13,000 Greeks (Xenophon among them), and marched inland toward the Euphrates before the Persians suspected anything. Artaxerxes assembled a far larger army, and the two met at Cunaxa on the Euphrates in 401 BC. Fortune at first favoured Cyrus, but he fell among enemy troops and was killed in single combat with his brother, which ended the war. The next page continues with the later reign of Artaxerxes II. Nothing is computed and no problem is served. The hand and content (a world-history lecture in the style of a Göttingen history course) suggest school or student notes, possibly not by Gauss himself, despite the bundle label 'HB.Lagrange1816'.
errors: Historical simplification: Cyrus the Younger was about 16–17 (not 15) when sent to Asia Minor in 408/407 BC, and he was older still at Cunaxa.
Historical simplification: Cyrus did not die in a formal duel. He charged Artaxerxes' bodyguard, wounded the king and was killed in the melee (Xenophon, Anabasis I.8; Plutarch, Artaxerxes).
The figure of 13,000 Greeks matches Xenophon's count (about 10,400 hoplites plus about 2,500 peltasts), so it is consistent with the sources.
